[MUQATIL:11:84-85/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Midyan was a son of Abraham, and Shuayb was son of Nuwayb, son of Midyan, son of Abraham.
[MUQATIL:11:84-85/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God sent Shuayb to Midyan; calling him their brother describes kinship, not shared religion.
[MUQATIL:11:84-85/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Worship God means affirm His oneness; they have no lord other than Him.
[MUQATIL:11:84-85/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Shuayb forbids short measure and weight when they measure and weigh; they are prosperous and blessed, yet he fears worldly punishment that will encompass them all.
[MUQATIL:11:84-85/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The encompassing day means punishment surrounded them so completely that none escaped.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When adjacent wāw and yāʾ meet in the described environments, they tend to become yāʾ because they share an articulation and yāʾ is lighter, resembling alif.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | prefers | Al-Khalīl analyzes سيد as فيعل, allowing a morphological pattern restricted to weak roots; Sībawayh prefers this account, supported by other weak-only forms and unbroken فتح in هيبان وتيحان.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · غيره | reports | Another analysis also calls سيد فيعل but explains its altered vowel by analogy with forms whose vowel changes when a noun changes; Sībawayh favors al-Khalīl's weak-root pattern analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ميت, هين, and لين, the medial weak consonant is deleted; the same deletion occurs in longer weak forms such as كينونة and قيدودة to avoid a crowd of yāʾ sounds.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as ديار and قيام reflect waw-to-yāʾ change from underlying ديوار and قيوام; قيوم and ديور similarly reflect underlying doubled-vowel forms on فيعال and فيعول.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Waw is not changed in صيود and طويل when the first of the adjacent letters is moving: assimilation requires the first letter to be still, so the original form remains.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A nonroot waw inserted by the pattern in سوير and بويع is not assimilated, since it can disappear in related forms; قوول and تقوول preserve length rather than merging the waws.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | Some speakers say ريا and رية, treating the waw left after dropping hamza as original; Sībawayh distinguishes this from سوير, whose waw substitutes for alif.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبالواوفيهياءإذاكانتمتحركةوالياءقبلهاساكنة#783/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The yāʾ of ديوان is not integral: its plural and diminutive recover waw, so it does not trigger assimilation; a true فيعال formation would assimilate.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When ظن, حسب, خال, أرى, رأى, or زعم is operative, it governs like other verbs; its object and predicate can both be accusative, including under fronting or questions.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In عبد الله أظنه منطلق, the pronoun can refer to the implicit source ذاك الظن rather than Abdullah; explicit ذاك is clearer and preferable to ظني.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When أن supplies a sufficient complement, ظننت أنه منطلق can be shortened to أظن أنه فاعل and needs no second predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In a reply to من تظن, ظننت زيدا means I suspect or accuse Zayd; ظنين likewise means accused.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh says ذاك is not used in the same way with حسب, خال, and أرى, since Arabic may admit a construction with one verb but not its semantic peers.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Interrogative pronouns such as أيهم, من, and ما are themselves clause beginnings; the verb normally follows them directly, with an object after it accusative, while poetry may front that object by necessity.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | These verbs can be canceled parenthetically, leaving the following predicate nominative; delaying the verb makes cancellation strongest because the statement begins in certainty before doubt is added.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · اللعين | reports | Al-Laʿīn's line about the rajaz poems uses خلت parenthetically, with اللؤم والخور nominative; it illustrates canceled government.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو ذؤيب | reports | Abū Dhuʾayb's تزعميني and al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī's أزعمك are poetic evidence that زعم can remain operative and govern its complements.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In questions with أين or هل, the interrogative does not prevent the following material from being analyzed as an initial clause; forms such as أين ترى زيدا allow the relevant accusative or nominative patterns.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | قال introduces a complete quoted utterance, so the quotation retains its independent syntax; the angels' statement to Mary consequently takes إن الله, not أن الله. | mentions 3:42
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Interrogative تقول is treated like تظن, not ظننت: speakers usually ask about their own belief, while the basic role of قال is to introduce an independent quotation.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو الخطاب | reports | A dialect of Banū Sulaym, whose Arabic Sībawayh trusts, treats the باب قلت like ظننت and its government.
[SIBAWAYH:فهىظنتتوحسبتوخلتوأريتورأيتوزعمتومايتصرفمنأفعالهن#61/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The verbal noun ظن can also be canceled; it is awkward sentence initially, but more acceptable after interrogative material or an existing clause.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · الجاحظ | reports | Al-Jahiz says no Kharijite or Jamaʿi on earth knew all the sciences better than Abu ʿUbayda.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The editor presents Abu ʿUbayda's breadth and depth through testimony that in each field he seemed to know no other and excelled at it.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-Aṣmaʿī and Abū Zayd were Abu ʿUbayda's contemporaries; their ordinary scholarly disagreements did not undermine trust or prevent recognition of truth.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The introduction says these scholars did not fabricate or exaggerate, explaining why their disagreements did not compromise confidence in their reports.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r5] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | rejects | The introduction rejects as an outlier a Western researchers' claim that Abu ʿUbayda fabricated material when his knowledge failed him.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · الرواة والآخذون عنهم | reports | Narrators and students preferred Abu ʿUbayda over one or both peers, although al-Aṣmaʿī's polished style won him some reported contests.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The introduction suggests Abu ʿUbayda's linguistic flexibility and freedom explain that preference, while noting his agreement with Abū Zayd on many issues.
[MAJAZ:v1p1#9/r8] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Abu ʿUbayda and Abū Zayd agreed on many linguistic questions.
[MAJAZ:v1p296/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Madyan is indeclinable because it is a feminine name. The phrase is elliptical for “to the people of Midian,” like “ask the town” or “ask the caravan,” meaning its people. | mentions 12:82
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p311#4/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda explains their good fortune as the good things and adornments of worldly life.
[TAB-FULL:v12p537#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Allah sent Shuaib to the people of Midian as their brother.
[TAB-FULL:v12p537#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Worship Allah by obeying Him and humbling yourselves before His commands and prohibitions; only He deserves worship.
[TAB-FULL:v12p537#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Shuaib forbids them to reduce people's due share in measures and weights.
[TAB-FULL:v12p537#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas takes their good fortune as low prices and interprets the encompassing day's punishment as high prices.
[TAB-FULL:v12p537#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan is reported to explain their good fortune as low prices.
[TAB-FULL:v12p537#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | In another report, al-Hasan says they had prosperity and low prices.
[TAB-FULL:v12p537#2/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada takes their good fortune to mean worldly goods, adornment, and visible worldly luxury.
[TAB-FULL:v12p540/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says their good fortune was worldly prosperity, noting that people call wealth خير in the phrase about leaving wealth in 2:180. | mentions 2:180

-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari prefers the broad sense of worldly good, including wealth, adornment, low prices, and every worldly blessing mentioned by the interpreters, rather than one blessing alone; they had ample provision, low prices, and much wealth.
[TAB-FULL:v12p540/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Shuaib warns that disobeying Allah and cheating people of their due could bring a day whose punishment completely encompasses them.
[TAB-FULL:v12p540/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Although محيط grammatically describes the day, it describes the punishment in meaning, since the punishment occurs on that day; al-Tabari compares the construction to calling a garment burned.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The underlying wording is sent to the people of Midian; the word people is omitted and Midian stands in its place.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Midian may name either the city or the tribe, which explains why it is treated as diptote.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2070#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says God sent Shuayb to Midian and to the people of al-Aykah, a wooded thicket.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2070#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · خلف بن حوشب | reports | Khalaf ibn Hawshab says Shuayb's people perished over cheating by tiny amounts, taking with heavy weights and giving with lighter ones.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2070#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says Midian's people disbelieved and defrauded measures and weights; after Shuayb called them and they rejected him, they persisted and asked for punishment.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2070#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says Shuayb saw them with an outward coating of worldly possessions and adornment.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2070#2/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم | reports | Ibn Zayd interprets their good as worldly wealth, noting that God calls wealth good in another verse. | mentions 2:180
[NAHHAS:v2p298/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Madyan is diptote because it is the name of a city.
[BAQILLANI:v1p122/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Literary experts can distinguish poets' styles, genuine invention, imitation, revision, and natural composition, just as experts recognize who made a textile.
[BAQILLANI:v1p122/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu Amr calls Zuhayr and al-Hutay'a servants of poetry because they revised it rather than composing spontaneously; Zuhayr called his polished long poems the revised annuals.
[BAQILLANI:v1p122/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Adi ibn al-Riqa's poem compares correcting a poem's flaws to a craftsperson straightening a spear; Suwayd ibn Kura depicts waiting at the gates of rhyme to hunt a verse.
[BAQILLANI:v1p122/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Some poets compose rapidly and naturally, without effort, and can equal those who labor over their verse.
[BAQILLANI:v1p122/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda transmits Abu Amr's account of Zuhayr and al-Hutay'a and ranks Zuhayr highest in praise and most controlled in verse.
[BAQILLANI:v1p122/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · الفرزدق | reports | A report says al-Farazdaq claimed a line he had appropriated from Jarir because it sounded like his own poetry.
[BAQILLANI:v1p125/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | A reader unable to perceive the Quran's eloquence exposes his own limited understanding; a true expert recognizes its distinction through careful contemplation.
[BAQILLANI:v1p125/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Readers of middling skill must defer to specialists, while only a few can judge this art; each craft has its own knowledgeable practitioners.
[BAQILLANI:v1p125/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Bāqillānī proposes comparing Quran and human compositions to expose differences in wisdom, law, unseen knowledge, worldly and religious benefit, certainty, eloquence, and verbal craft.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | Repeating “khidr” in “khidr Unayza” serves only the meter and adds no beauty or stylistic force.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r10] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | The couplet is so lewd and indecent that a noble person would disdain to say or mention it.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | The hemistich imports women’s colloquial speech into the poem and offers nothing beyond that transcription.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | Repeating the woman’s statement as “she says” after “she said” is redundant, metrically motivated, and ugly; the first report suffices.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The second hemistich likewise uses feminine speech.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu ʿUbayda explains that the poet says “my camel,” not “my she-camel,” because women were carried on stronger male camels.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | Bāqillānī questions Abu ʿUbayda: baʿīr most likely names either sex, and the poet needed it for the meter.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r7] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | The first line of the next couplet is competently woven but has no striking meaning or noble diction, resembling low-grade craft.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r8] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Grammarians object to “a pregnant woman like you I visited”; supplying rabb (“perhaps”) makes sense of the boast that he distracts pregnant and nursing women from their children.
[BAQILLANI:v1p166/r9] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | The second line does not support the request not to send him away: his boast of seducing women instead gives her reason to shun and despise him.
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The first line praises the woman for rising with the poet to leave in private and for trailing a patterned cloak behind her.
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | “Murajjal” refers to a kind of brocade, whose ornamentation is called tarjīl.
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | “Behind us, in our wake” is redundant: the wake alone suffices, and a garment’s train necessarily trails behind its wearer.
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | The poet should have used the singular “tail of a cloak,” rather than plural “tails.”
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Even allowing for its faults, the line is merely good; Ibn al-Muʿtazz wrote a better version of the idea.
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | In the next line, ajaznā means “we crossed”; khabt is a low-lying tract, ḥiqāf a curved dune, and ʿaqanqal intertwined, compact sand.
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r7] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | The obscure word ʿaqanqal breaks the preceding smooth, colloquial style and adds no useful effect.
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r8] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Unusual, difficult diction is praiseworthy when it fits its subject, as in the Qurʾānic description of the grim day; elsewhere it is blameworthy. | mentions 76:10
[BAQILLANI:v1p176/r9] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | reports | A caliph of the Umayyads reportedly delighted as Jarīr recited his poem, then reached the line addressing Būzaʿ and mocked the listener.
[SULAMI:v1p323#4/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The closest condition to being gradually ensnared is security, ease, and a succession of blessings and good things.
[SULAMI:v1p323#4/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Being seen in goodness means receiving God's favor; the feared danger is falling short in gratitude for it.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Madyan here is the people of Shuʿayb.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Though guilty of shirk, they also cheated in measures; belief calls them to abandon shirk and full measure forbids cheating.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس والحسن | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan take “in good condition” to mean low prices.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · قتادة وابن زيد | reports | Qatāda and Ibn Zayd take it to mean wealth and worldly adornment.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r13] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A further possible sense is abundant crops and earnings.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r14] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس والحسن | reports | On the low-price reading of “in good condition,” the warning can mean fear of high prices.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r15] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another possibility is worldly punishment of total destruction.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r16] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The warning can also mean the punishment of the Fire in the afterlife.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One account says they are the sons of Madyan son of Abraham; the tribal ancestor’s name stands for his descendants, as with Muḍar.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Madyan may be a foreign name or, alternatively, an Arabic one.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | If it is a city name, it may derive from madana, “to reside in a place,” with the yāʾ treated as extra.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | If it is a man’s name, it may derive from dānat, “to rule or possess,” with the mīm treated as extra.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Shuʿayb is a diminutive of shaʿb, which can mean a mountain path.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p494/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another proposed sense of shaʿb is a great tribe.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p520/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عامة المفسرين | reports | Most commentators understand their good fortune as blessing, fertility, abundant wealth, and worldly adornment.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p520/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | One explanation is that Shuayb warned that cheating would bring high prices, lost blessing, and punishment if they did not repent.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p520/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says not to diminish measures when God has blessed them with abundant wealth and low prices; they have no need to short measure.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p520/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The threatened punishment will encompass them so that no one escapes.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p520/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Although مُحيط grammatically describes the day, it means the punishment, since the encompassing day of punishment means the punishment encompasses them.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:84-87/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The opening of this account was explained in Surat al-Aʿrāf. | mentions 7:85
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:84-87/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | They enjoy prosperity and fertility; with God's blessings, money, and low prices, they have no need to cheat in measures.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:84-87/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | He warns of a punishment that will surround them so none can escape.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p110/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Putting the subject before its verb can claim exclusive agency: أنا كتبت and أنا شفعت rebut doubt that someone else performed the action.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p110/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Fronting can instead establish certainty without excluding others; هم يفرشون describes the riders’ habitual conduct, with the subject named first to prevent doubt or mistaken attribution.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p144/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A second form of restriction confines a qualified kind of predicate to its subject, rather than merely exaggerating or discounting others; qualification by time or object creates that distinct kind.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p144/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Aʿshā’s praise means the patron alone gives this special hundred-camel gift, repeatedly; it is a recurring kind of giving, unlike one particular departure.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p144/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The author distinguishes a recurring type of action from one specific act: جرير هو القائل asserts that Jarīr composed this particular verse, so repetition is not at issue.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p144/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The author begins a third form of restriction that does not confine the predicate’s whole genus to the subject, unlike زيد هو الشجاع; the excerpt cuts off before its next comparison.
[JISHUMI:v5p3548/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Muhit describes something encircling another like a wall; the related verb can also mean to contain or surround with care.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Shu'ayb is called their brother in kinship; Madyan may refer to the descendants of Midian son of Abraham.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says Madyan is the name of a city or a tribe.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو مسلم | reports | Abu Muslim says Madyan is the city's name, with its people intended.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Worship Allah means affirm His oneness and worship no other; the passage begins with tawhid because it is the most important duty and the foundation of the rest.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | They are forbidden to give short measure or weight in what they sell to others; they had been cheating in those transactions.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس، والحسن | reports | Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan interpret their being in good as low prices; Shu'ayb warns that prices may rise, blessings disappear, and punishment arrive.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قتادة، وابن زيد، والضحاك | reports | Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and al-Dahhak take the good to mean wealth and worldly adornment.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid understands their good condition as fertility and abundance.
[JISHUMI:v5p3549/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The punishment will envelop them all so that none escape; the day surrounds them with punishment instead of the blessings that currently surround them.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p194#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | God sent Shuʿayb to the descendants of Midian.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p194#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | They are told not to cheat or diminish measures and weights; they practiced this fraud alongside their polytheism.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p194#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says that Shuʿayb saw them enjoying prosperity and blessing.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p194#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid says they had fertile conditions and abundance.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p194#2/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Shuʿayb warned that their blessing could disappear, prices rise, and punishment arrive if they did not repent.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p194#2/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The encompassing day's punishment will surround and destroy them.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p393#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Shuʿayb may mean they possess ample wealth and therefore need not cheat in measures.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p393#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Alternatively, they enjoy God's blessing, which should be met with conduct other than fraud.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p393#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Alternatively, they are already in a good state and should not destroy it through their conduct, as in the speech of Pharaoh's believing man (40:29). | mentions 40:29
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p393#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | A day encompassing them is a destructive day; the wording echoes the destruction of the garden in 18:42 and originally evokes enemy encirclement. | mentions 18:42
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p393#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | prefers | Calling the day encompassing is more forceful than calling the punishment so, because the day contains events and its encompassing torment gathers all it contains upon the sufferer.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The wording implies ‘We sent their brother Shuayb to Midian,’ with ‘sent’ understood.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet said that whenever a people short-measure and short-weigh, their provision is withheld; Ibn Atiyya cites this in support, without grading it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | Another view takes ‘good’ as all God’s blessings and the punishment as the destruction that ultimately befell them.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | One view takes Midian as a place, making the phrase mean the people of Midian, as in the idiom ‘ask the town.’ | mentions 10:42
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | Another view locates the Midian region in the area of Syria.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | A further view makes Midian the name of a man whose descendants formed the tribe; the name is indeclinable either way.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · النقاش | reports | Al-Naqqash says Midian was Abraham’s biological son; Ibn Atiyya rejects this as remote because Shuayb is said to be Arab and Arabs connect to Abraham only through Ishmael.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Shuayb’s call shows they worshipped idols, confirmed by their later words; disbelief, not sin, merited their annihilation, since God annihilates no nation except for disbelief. | mentions 11:87
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | They agreed to give outsiders short measure and weight while taking full measure from them; accompanying sin was secondary to their disbelief.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الزجاج | reports | Zajjaj’s book suggests that the people had agreed among themselves to defraud one another.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p198#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains ‘in prosperity’ as low prices and the encompassing day’s punishment as ruinous high prices.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p199/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Calling the day encompassing is f

[TABRISI:11:87/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Wazn is adjusting one thing against another for lightness or heaviness by a measuring instrument; metrical poetry is adjusted by prosody.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p287/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | In Shuyayb’s statement “I see you in prosperity,” al-khayr means low or favorable prices.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The root’s original sense is striking or flogging with a whip or similar implement.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r11] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · شيخنا | reports | The source’s teacher derives laughter from splitting open, as when the earth opens to bring forth plants.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r12] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · شيخنا | reports | Laughter names the opening of the mouth in smiling or guffawing; he treats it as distinctive to human beings among animals lacking speech.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r13] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعضهم | reports | One definition describes laughter as a natural expansion of the rational soul, showing its response to something delightful.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r14] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · ابن فارس | reports | Ibn Fāris says al-ḍāḥika is any tooth visible in front of the molars when laughing.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r15] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Al-ḍaḥūk is a clear road and al-uḍḥūka is something laughed at; ḍaḥka with a still ḥāʾ is someone mocked, while ḍaḥika with a vowel is someone who laughs often.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | By metaphor, ḍaraba can mean to travel; ḍārib can also mean someone practicing a trade.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Al-ḍarb can describe a slight-built man; the cited verse calls the speaker a known, quick, keen man.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Al-ḍarb also means a kind or class of things.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | With fatḥa on the second radical, al-ḍarab means thick honey.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | A ḍarība is a tax or other levy imposed on a person.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p400/r7] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Aḍraba ʿan al-amr means to desist from a matter; ḍarb can also mean a parable.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Ibn al-Jawzī refers the account of Midian to his earlier explanation at al-Aʿrāf 85. | mentions 7:85
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Shuʿayb forbids short measure and weight; his people practiced fraud despite their unbelief.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن العباس والحسن ومجاهد | reports | Ibn al-ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid understand their good condition as low prices.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس وقتادة وابن زيد | reports | Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās, along with Qatāda and Ibn Zayd, takes it as abundant wealth; al-Farrāʾ notes they had much wealth and cheap prices.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ argues that their plentiful wealth and low prices left them no need to cheat in weighing and measuring.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس ومجاهد | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the encompassing punishment is high prices; Mujāhid specifies drought, famine, and high prices.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil says the threat is a worldly punishment, the one that later struck them.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p147/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الماوردي | reports | Al-Māwardī gives the third interpretation: the punishment of the Fire in the afterlife.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | This is the sixth narrative recounted in the sūra.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The day is grammatically described as encompassing, while the punishment is what it encompasses by metaphor, as in 11:77. | mentions 11:77
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Madyan was Abraham’s son, whose name later denoted the tribe; on this reading, the verse addresses the people of Madyan.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · كثير من المفسرين | reports | Many exegetes identify Madyan as a city founded by Madyan son of Abraham; the verse then omits أهل, meaning its inhabitants.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prophets begin by calling people to monotheism, then address the next most pressing matter; Shuʿayb accordingly first called them to worship God alone.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because short measure was customary in Madyan, Shuʿayb next forbade it; the wrong could be giving less when measuring for others or taking more than due, both reducing another’s right.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One reading is a warning that prices will rise and blessing disappear unless they repent of cheating.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, God has already granted them wealth, low prices, and abundance, so they have no need to cheat in measure.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas interprets ‘I fear’ as ‘I know’: the encompassing punishment will occur.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p33/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · آخرون | reports | Others take it as genuine fear: because they may abandon the practice from fear of punishment, Shuʿayb’s statement expresses expectation rather than certain knowledge.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p34/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | One view identifies the encompassing punishment as the Day of Resurrection, appointed for the punishment of the condemned.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p34/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Another view includes punishment in both this world and the next.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p34/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | A third view means the worldly punishment of total destruction, as for other prophets’ peoples.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p34/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Razi says the phrase encompasses every punishment, surrounding them from every side like a circle surrounds what is inside; this intensifies the threat, as in 18:42. | mentions 18:42
[RAZI-FULL:v18p34/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Repeating the command is emphatic because the people persisted in the cheating and needed strong insistence.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p34/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Forbidding short measure and commanding full measure are distinct; joining prohibition and its opposite’s command reinforces the warning, like commanding kinship and forbidding severance.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p34/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Razi rejects the claim that the prohibition alone entails the command: some might regard all commerce as inseparable from fraud, so the positive command clarifies that trade is permitted when rights are fulfilled.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Shuʿayb was sent to Madyan, the people of Shuʿayb.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Calling the day encompassing means its punishment will surround them, like calling a day severe to mean its heat is severe.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | One view identifies the punishment as the fire of the afterlife.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Another view identifies it as earthly destruction.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | A third view, related from Ibn ʿAbbās, takes the punishment to mean high prices.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي | reports | The Prophet said that when a people openly cheat in measure and weight, God afflicts them with drought and high prices; no grading is given.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | One view identifies Madyan as the descendants of Madyan son of Abraham, using the name for his offspring as Mudar can mean the descendants of Mudar.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A second view takes Madyan as the name of their city, from which its inhabitants were named.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النحاس | reports | Al-Naḥḥās says Madyan is indeclinable because it is a city name.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | They cheated when buying and selling: they took excess measure from food sellers but gave food buyers short measure, so they were commanded to abandon shirk and fraud.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | When buying they demanded the greatest possible measure, but when selling they gave less and withheld as much as possible.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The command to worship God makes them leave shirk, while the command to fulfill measure makes them leave cheating.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Shuʿayb sees them enjoying ample provision and many blessings.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-86/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says their good circumstances meant prices were low.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:11:84/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Madyan may mean the descendants of Madyan son of Abraham or the town he built and named for himself.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:11:84/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, it refers to the town’s inhabitants.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:11:84/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | He begins with monotheism as the foundation, then forbids short measure and weight as unjust and destructive of fair exchange.
